ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a hexagon with a thick black edge, and many black diagonals are drawn inside; three long diagonals connecting opposite vertices intersect at the center point, dividing the hexagon into six triangular sectors around the center. The pink and yellow regions show that these lines further cut each sector into small pieces, and the whole presents a repeated symmetric pattern. Reasoning: Record the vertices in order by coordinates as A=(0,0), B=(1,0), C=(2,1), D=(2,2), E=(1,2), F=(0,1). The three diagonals of opposite vertices AD, BE, CF intersect at O=(1,1). From the repeated sector structure and coordinate symmetry in the figure, it is only necessary to analyze one sector triangle ABO. In triangle ABO, there are also two related diagonal segments in the figure: AC and BF. The line AC from A=(0,0) to C=(2,1) can be written as (2t,t), and it intersects BO, namely x=1, at P=(1,1/2). The line BF from B=(1,0) to F=(0,1) can be written as (1-s,s), and it intersects AO, namely y=x, at Q=(1/2,1/2). When the two lines AC and BF intersect, (2t,t)=(1-s,s), giving t=s=1/3, so the intersection point R=(2/3,1/3). These points divide triangle ABO into four pieces. Area calculation: the area of triangle AQR is 1/12; the area of triangle BRP is 1/12; the area of triangle ABR is 1/6; the area of the remaining quadrilateral QOPR is the area 1/2 of triangle ABO minus the areas of the first three pieces, namely 1/2-1/12-1/12-1/6=1/6. Therefore the areas of all regions will only be 1/12 or 1/6. The minimum area a=1/12, and the maximum area b=1/6, so a:b=(1/12):(1/6)=1:2.

method.method_draft: Use the three long diagonals as a symmetry framework. From the image, note that the opposite-vertex diagonals meet at the center and divide the hexagon into six congruent-looking triangular sectors; in the coordinates these are exactly triangles such as A=(0,0), B=(1,0), and O=(1,1), where O is the intersection of AD, BE, and CF. Work in one sector, say triangle ABO. The image shows two additional diagonal segments crossing inside this sector: AC from A to the opposite side BO and BF from B to the side AO. Using the text coordinates, compute their intersection points: AC meets BO at (1,1/2), BF meets AO at (1/2,1/2), and AC intersects BF at (2/3,1/3). These split triangle ABO into four regions. Use the shoelace formula or base-height calculations to find the two smaller triangular pieces have area 1/12 and the two larger pieces have area 1/6. By the repeated sector pattern visible in the diagram and by the coordinate symmetry of the hexagon, every region is congruent or equal-area to one of these pieces. Thus the smallest-to-largest area ratio is (1/12):(1/6)=1:2.

The side equations are AB: y=0, BC: y=x-1, CD: x=2, DE: y=2, EF: y=x+1, FA: x=0. The line BF from B=(1,0) to F=(0,1) can be written as (1-s,s), and it intersects AO, namely y=x, at Q=(1/2,1/2). When the two lines AC and BF intersect, (2t,t)=(1-s,s), giving t=s=1/3, so the intersection point R=(2/3,1/3).
These points divide triangle ABO into four pieces. Therefore the areas of all regions will only be 1/12 or 1/6. The minimum area a=1/12, and the maximum area b=1/6, so a:b=(1/12):(1/6)=1:2.
